title: Erasmus
hookLine: a scholar prints the Greek New Testament and wants the ploughboy singing scripture

lines: GREEK ON ONE SIDE, LATIN ON THE OTHER.
cards: Proof sheets, the ink still wet, spread across a table in a printer's shop in Basel. A priest leans over them, correcting as fast as they come. Each page has two columns.
On one side, the New Testament in Greek, the language its writers used. On the other, a fresh Latin translation he has made himself.
Readers who've known the gospels all their lives in one familiar Latin wording can now check it against the Greek, line by line. Some will be thrilled. Some will be furious.

teach.b: Desiderius Erasmus was a priest and scholar from Rotterdam who traveled widely, writing letters, editing old books, and poking fun at the church he loved.
He belonged to a movement called humanism, and its rallying cry was two Latin words: ad fontes. To the springs. Back to the sources.
Drink the water where it comes out of the rock, not after it has run down a long pipe. For Erasmus, the spring was the Greek of the New Testament, and the early Christian writers who read it.
So he gathered Greek manuscripts, compared them, and printed a Greek text beside his own Latin. Where his Latin differed from the familiar wording, some readers were alarmed.
His answer, roughly: loving the text means looking hard at it. In the preface, a little essay he called the Paraclesis, the exhortation, he says something that still sounds bold.
He wishes the scriptures could be read by everyone, women too, and turned into every language.

teach.h: THE FARMER SINGING AT THE PLOUGH.
teach.b: He pictures the farmer singing a piece of it behind the plough, the weaver humming it at the loom, the traveler shortening the road with its stories. Erasmus stayed in the Catholic church all his life.
He wanted it cleaned up from the inside, by learning and by plain imitation of Christ, not torn apart. Soon others would take his Greek text and his questions much further than he ever meant to go.
A saying went around that Erasmus laid the egg and Luther hatched it. Erasmus did not enjoy that one.

how: Christians in many churches study the Bible alongside its Greek and Hebrew, and comparing translations side by side is a common part of Bible study groups and sermon preparation.

practice: Take the angels' song from Luke: the King James Bible says, "on earth peace, good will toward men," and the Douay-Rheims, an old Catholic English translation, says, "on earth peace to men of good will."

Say each slowly in your head, and notice where they meet and where they part, without deciding which is right, the way Erasmus set his two columns side by side. If you pray, rest on whichever line speaks to you.
